newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel says Bonn may raise borrowing to fill gap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel says Bonn may raise borrowing to fill gap.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday the government may have to increase new borrowing for 1997 because of persistently high unemployment, but said he was certain Germany would qualify for the single European currency.

Waigel said the government was waiting for a report on 1997 tax revenues due on Thursday. If the tax income is less than expected and opens new holes in the budget, Waigel said the government had a variety of measures on hand to fill the gaps.

"We will do everything we can to fulfill the Maastricht criteria and we will fulfill them," Waigel told jounalists in Bonn of the criteria for European monetary union EMU set in the European Union's Maastricht Treaty.
"We are prepared with a number of corresponding measures (if tax revenues are down)."

High unemployment is straining German budgets and hurting Germany's chances of qualifying for EMU. The euro is scheduled to be launched in 1999 by countries that meet the targets in 1997 that include limits on budget deficits, public debt and inflation.

Waigel said the coalition "would do everything it could to avoid tax increases" to fill the budget holes. He said new borrowing on top of the 53.4 billion marks ($31 billion) in debt already included in the 1997 budget "cannot be ruled out."

A Reuters survey of 35 European economists published on Wednesday showed Germany was the only country failing to make progress on achieving or bettering the Maastricht convergence targets set for membership in monetary union.
Asked by reporters whether the new debt was necessary, Waigel said the high costs of supporting four million unemployed meant that new borrowing "would be a logicial consequence of the facts."

Waigel, speaking to journalists at a book presentation in Bonn, said that the government was also considering selling part of its 75 percent stake in telecoms giant Deutsche Telekom AG earlier than the originally planned date of 2000. The $13 billion sale of an inital 25 percent in November had no impact on government finances as the revenues went to the company itself.
"With the company's exquisite state of health a sale of shares would not be a problem," Waigel said.
Waigel said Bonn's unemployment payments depended in part on the development of the labour market, and that was something he could not influence.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition met on Tuesday to discuss how best to plug gaps in the 1997 budget as other officials were at a three-day session to estimate the tax shortfall.
Federal, state and central bank officials were meeting with private-sector advisors in a semiannual closed-door conference in the east German town of Schwerin to hammer out hard numbers.
Opposition officials have said 1997 taxes could be running as much as 20 billion marks ($12 billion) below budget projections, mainly due to high unemployment.
Germany, like other European nations, is under pressure to reduce its government deficit to three percent of total economic output this year, to qualify for EMU.
The federal budget foresees a deficit of 53.4 billion marks for 1997, in line with the EMU goal, but many observers are sceptical it can hit the mark.
"We expect a tax revenue shortfall this year and it will be difficult to implement further cuts given high levels of unemployment," said Gernot Nerb, senior economist at Salomon Brothers Germany.

Otto Lambsdorff, a leader of the centrist Free Democrats that share power with Kohl's Christian Democrats, told the Cologne Express newspaper he expects the tax revenues for 1997 to be 20 billion marks less than expected.

"There will be a hole of about 20 billion marks," Lambsdorff said. "A certain shortfall of about eight billion has most likely already been factored in so there will be a hole of about 12 billion marks to fill."

Lambsdorff added: "The FDP will not accept tax increases...The missing money has to be saved in the current budget, if necessary with a spending freeze. A slightly higher increase in borrowing is better than tax increases."
Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of the FDP, said the FDP would strictly oppose new taxes to plug the holes.
"That would be poison for the economy," Gerhardt said.

In a separate magazine interview, Gerhardt said that the stability of the euro would not be considerably undermined if Germany's budget deficit slighly exceeded the Maastricht targets, a position Waigel has stridently rejected. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
